title: Agile product management, transition to operations and DevOps
blurb: Explain what happens beyond the project: agile product management, a smooth transition to operations, and continuous agile development and operations.
question: A project has delivered a new app. How should it be handed over so agile practices continue, and how should later enhancements be managed?

teach.body: A project is temporary, but its product carries on being used, supported and improved. PRINCE2 Agile looks beyond the project at three things: agile product management after delivery, the transition from the project to operations, and continuous agile development and operations, where improvements keep flowing to users quickly and safely.

Agile product management is the strategic and tactical management of product development using agile frameworks such as Scrum and Kanban. The product manager keeps a high-level product vision and a flexible roadmap, adjusted continually from stakeholder, customer and market feedback. Enhancements after the project are handled through product management iterations rather than by starting a new project for each one.

head: Feature
In practice
rows: High-level vision; flexible roadmap adjusted from feedback
Short cycles; rank by business value, user feedback, market
Work closely with development, design, stakeholders
Iterative planning and adaptation; each release adds value
teach.caption: Paraphrased from 14.2.2.1.

teach.body: Handover needs more than a go-live date. Agile artifacts and tools are handed over so agile practices stay aligned after transition. Tailored training with manuals, quick-start guides and videos helps users adopt the product. Explicit step-by-step operational procedures support consistent maintenance. Escalation pathways help knowledge transfer, and regular feedback loops such as surveys and retrospectives give actionable insights.

teach.h: Handover element and what it achieves
head: Element
Main effect
teach.caption: Paraphrased from 14.2.1.

teach.body: This is a set of practices for rapid, automated delivery of new features, fixes and improvements, so the product is always deployable and keeps improving with minimal manual intervention. With DevOps, development, testing and operations collaborate closely so releases are seamless and automated. Continuous Delivery ships small, incremental changes for fast feedback from real users, and monitoring in production feeds back into development.

Saltmarsh District Council's parking app goes live at the end of the project. The team hands its product backlog, team dashboard and pipeline tools to the council's digital service team, runs short training sessions with quick-start guides for wardens, and writes step-by-step support procedures with SLAs. Product manager Imogen Clarke keeps a flexible roadmap, adds monthly user surveys, and the team ships small updates weekly, watching production data for slow payment screens.

teach.text: Each handover element has its own job: training and guides drive ADOPTION; procedures and SLAs support MAINTENANCE; feedback loops collect INSIGHTS; handing over agile artifacts and tools keeps AGILE PRACTICES aligned. And product enhancements go through product management iterations, not a new project each time.

items: Agile product management: vision with a flexible, feedback-driven roadmap.
Short cycles prioritized by business value, user feedback and market needs.
Transition: hand over agile artifacts and tools, training, procedures, escalation paths, feedback loops.
Continuous development and operations: rapid, automated, always deployable.
DevOps: development, testing and operations collaborate closely.
Continuous Delivery: small increments, fast feedback from real users.

summary: You can now explain agile product management, what a good transition to operations hands over, and how continuous agile development and operations keep a product improving. You can also match each handover element to the effect it has.

A.q: In agile product management, how is the product roadmap treated?
options: Kept flexible, adjusted from stakeholder and market feedback
Fixed at the start and changed through formal change control
Owned by operations and reviewed at each annual budget
Replaced by the project's release map after handover
A.why: The product manager keeps a high-level vision and a flexible roadmap, adjusted continually from feedback (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.1: A fixed roadmap contradicts agile product management.
whyNot.2: The roadmap is adjusted continually, not on an annual cycle.
whyNot.3: The release map is a project artifact; the product roadmap continues after the project.

A.q: Which handover element mainly keeps the product's operation aligned with agile practices after transition?
options: Escalation pathways
Operational procedures
Feedback mechanisms
Agile artifacts and tools
A.why: Handing over agile artifacts and tools gives continuity and alignment with agile practices after transition (14.2.1).

whyNot.0: Escalation pathways help knowledge transfer and issue handling.
whyNot.1: Procedures support consistent maintenance and clear expectations.
whyNot.2: Feedback mechanisms give real-time insights and allow adjustments.

A.q: What is continuous agile development and operations?
options: Large, planned releases after full regression testing
Practices for rapid, automated delivery of features and fixes
A final project stage dedicated to operational acceptance
A governance board that approves each deployment by hand
A.why: It is a set of practices for rapid, automated delivery of features, fixes and improvements, keeping the product deployable (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Continuous delivery favours small, frequent increments.
whyNot.2: It operationalizes agile practices continually, not as a single stage.
whyNot.3: The aim is minimal manual intervention, not manual approval of each release.

B.q: Which handover element mainly provides actionable insights that drive ongoing improvement?
options: Quick-start guides and video tutorials
Maintenance schedules in the procedures
Regular feedback loops such as user surveys
Escalation pathways with named contacts
B.why: Regular feedback loops such as surveys and retrospectives collect actionable insights (14.2.1).

whyNot.3: Escalation pathways help knowledge transfer and issue resolution.

B.q: In DevOps, how do development, testing and operations work?
options: As separate teams with formal hand-offs
In close collaboration so release is seamless and automated
With operations approving changes at a monthly board
With testing done by operations after deployment
B.why: With DevOps, development, testing and operations collaborate closely so releases are seamless and automated (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Silos and formal hand-offs are what DevOps removes.
whyNot.2: Monthly approval boards slow the rapid, automated delivery DevOps aims for.
whyNot.3: Testing is part of the automated flow before release.

B.q: After the project, users ask for further enhancements to the product. What approach fits PRINCE2 Agile guidance?
options: Start a new project for each enhancement
Freeze the product until the next budget year
Reconvene the original project board for each request
Handle them through product management iterations
B.why: Agile product management manages the product through iterations; a new project per enhancement is not appropriate (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Projects are temporary; ongoing enhancement belongs to product management.
whyNot.1: Freezing the product delays value and feedback.
whyNot.2: The project board ends with the project; product management takes over.

C.q:
Which two statements about continuous agile development and operations are correct?
1. Continuous Delivery releases small, incremental changes for fast feedback from real users.
2. The product is deployed once, at project closure.
3. Monitoring in production feeds back into development.
4. Tailored end-user training mainly sets out the SLAs.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
C.why: Continuous Delivery ships small increments for fast feedback, and production monitoring informs development (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: the product is kept always deployable and released often.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: releases are frequent, and SLAs belong in operational procedures.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: training supports adoption; SLAs belong in operational procedures.

C.q: Which handover element sets out configuration management, maintenance schedules, SLAs and troubleshooting guides, and what does it achieve?
options: Escalation pathways; faster knowledge transfer
Feedback loops; actionable insights for change
Operational procedures; smooth, consistent maintenance
End-user training; wider user adoption
C.why: Step-by-step operational procedures support smooth, consistent maintenance and clear operational expectations (14.2.1).

whyNot.0: Escalation pathways set contacts and timelines for resolving issues.
whyNot.1: Feedback loops gather insights from users and teams.
whyNot.3: Training, manuals and guides support adoption.

C.q: A product manager works in short cycles, ranking features by business value, user feedback and changing market needs. Which feature of agile product management is this?
options: Product vision and roadmap
Collaboration with development teams
Lifecycle management
Iteration and prioritization
C.why: Iteration and prioritization means short cycles with features ranked by business value, feedback and market needs (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.0: Vision and roadmap is about the long-term direction.
whyNot.1: Collaboration is about working with development, design and stakeholders.
whyNot.2: Lifecycle management is the overall iterative planning and adaptation.

reteach.title: A new bus route after launch day
reteach.question: What keeps a new bus route working well after the launch project ends?

blocks.h: Launch is the start of the service
blocks.body: The launch team hands over its timetable tools and planning boards to the depot, trains drivers, writes clear procedures for breakdowns, names who to call, and sets up passenger surveys. From then on, the route manager tweaks the timetable every few weeks based on how full the buses are and what passengers say.

blocks.h: Bus route to beyond the project
head: Bus route
PRINCE2 Agile

blocks.text: Tweaking the timetable is ongoing product management, not a new launch project each time.

explain.body: Agile product managers work closely with development, design and other stakeholders so the product meets both business objectives and user needs.

test.q: Agile product managers work closely with whom, so the product meets business objectives and user needs?
options: Operations staff at each yearly review
Development, design and other stakeholders
The project board as a standing committee
Senior suppliers through contract renegotiation
test.why: Close collaboration with development, design and other stakeholders is a key feature (14.2.2.1).

whyNot.2: The project board ends with the project.
whyNot.3: Contract renegotiation is not the collaboration described.

explain.body: Tailored end-user training, supported by manuals, quick-start guides and video tutorials, helps users take up the product.

test.q: What is the main purpose of tailored end-user training with manuals, quick-start guides and videos?
options: To help users adopt the product
To collect insights for improvement
To define the service levels
To set escalation timelines
test.why: Training and supporting materials facilitate user adoption (14.2.1).

whyNot.2: Service levels sit in operational procedures.
whyNot.3: Escalation pathways set contacts and timelines.

explain.body: Continuous agile development and operations keeps the product in a deployable state so it can be released and improved with minimal manual intervention.

test.q: What does it mean for a product to be 'always in a deployable state'?
options: It is released at each stage boundary by the board
Every change waits for one final, combined release
It can be released at any time with little manual effort
Operations hold a weekly board to approve releases
test.why: The product is always deployable and can be improved with minimal manual intervention (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Releases are not tied to stage boundaries.
whyNot.1: Waiting for one final release is the opposite.
whyNot.3: Manual release boards slow automated delivery.

explain.body: Monitoring performance, user behaviour and system health in production feeds back into development, closing the loop.

test.q: In continuous agile development and operations, what happens to production monitoring data?
options: It is archived for the next audit
It goes to the board in highlight reports
It is reviewed once at handover
It feeds back into development
test.why: Monitoring in production feeds back into development (14.2.2.2).

whyNot.0: Archiving alone would waste the feedback.
whyNot.1: Highlight reports are project products, replaced by the project dashboard.
whyNot.2: Monitoring is continual, not a one-off at handover.
